what: Streaming server-side rendering sends HTML in chunks as each part of the page becomes ready, instead of waiting for the whole page. Suspense boundaries mark where the page can show a fallback and fill in real content later.
like: Like a restaurant bringing the bread and starters straight away while the main course is still cooking, instead of serving everything at once at the end.
why: Users see the page shell right away, so first paint no longer waits for the slowest query
Slow sections do not block fast ones - each boundary streams on its own
Hydration can start per section, keeping the page responsive sooner

steps.d: The server renders everything above the Suspense boundaries - layout, nav and fallback skeletons - and flushes it first. TTFB drops to the time to render that shell.
Because the first chunk includes link and script tags, the browser fetches CSS, JS and fonts while the server is still waiting on data.

steps.t: Each boundary streams on its own
steps.d: When a boundary's data resolves, React sends its HTML plus a tiny inline script that swaps out the fallback. No JS bundle is needed for this swap.
React hydrates boundaries independently and prioritises the one the user interacts with, so one slow region does not freeze the rest.
The first chunk fixes the HTTP status at 200. If something fails later, the nearest error boundary renders in place; a real 404 must be decided before streaming starts.

numbers.l: React reveals suspended content at most once per 300 ms, so quick boundaries appear together
Safari/WebKit buffers a streamed response until it exceeds this size - only matters for tiny demos
rough good TTFB; streaming lowers it to the time to render the shell
status code sent with the first chunk and unchangeable afterwards

choices.d: Wrap each independent slow region in its own Suspense, close to the data. One big boundary becomes a full-page skeleton and loses the benefit.
If the hero image or main heading is inside a boundary it cannot paint until the swap. Keep it in the static shell and preload the LCP image.
Fallbacks with the same dimensions as the final content prevent layout shift (CLS) when the swap happens.
Reverse proxies (disable with X-Accel-Buffering: no), some CDNs, compression and serverless platforms can hold chunks back, wiping out the gain.

instead.why: Streaming is the delivery mechanism; RSC is how the server parts are written
If the page is the same for everyone, prebuild it and skip per-request rendering

breaks.d: A proxy, CDN or compression layer collects all chunks first.
breaks.see: Page appears all at once; Network tab shows no staggered chunks
breaks.fix: Disable proxy buffering, check CDN support, flush compression; verify with a stream-reading script

breaks.d: Hero content placed behind a Suspense boundary.
breaks.see: LCP element appears only after a late swap
breaks.fix: Render LCP content in the shell; preload the hero image

breaks.see: Soft 404: status 200 with an error page
breaks.fix: Check existence before any await or Suspense; Next.js adds noindex to streamed 404s as a fallback

say: I would stream: send the layout and skeletons immediately, then let each Suspense boundary fill in as its data resolves, so TTFB and first paint no longer depend on the slowest query.
I keep the LCP element out of Suspense, size the skeletons to avoid layout shift, and place a separate boundary around each independent data source.
I would also check that the proxy, CDN and compression do not buffer the response, because streaming only helps if chunks actually reach the browser.

followups.a: Streaming is still server-rendered HTML, so it does not hurt SEO by itself. Next.js resolves metadata before streaming for bots that only read static HTML, and uses noindex on streamed 404s.

followups.q: How is this different from fetching in useEffect?
followups.a: Data fetched in an Effect does not trigger Suspense and starts only after JS runs. Streaming starts the work on the server during the first request, and the HTML arrives with the data already rendered.

today: Frameworks now treat streaming as the default model: Next.js App Router streams around Suspense and loading.js automatically, and Cache Components prerenders a static shell at build time while dynamic parts stream in behind it.

check.q: What does the server send first in streaming SSR?
check.a: The static shell with Suspense fallbacks
d: The final HTML for the whole page
check.why: The shell lets the browser paint and start loading assets while slow data resolves.

check.q: Where should the hero image that is your LCP element go?
check.a: Outside Suspense boundaries, in the shell
check.why: Content inside a boundary can only paint after the swap, delaying LCP.

check.q: A page was found missing after streaming started. What status did the client get?
check.why: The status is fixed by the first chunk; check before streaming to return a real 404.
